title: Island endemics are related to species of the nearest continent

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Island endemics are related to species of the nearest continent

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: It is an almost universal rule that the endemic species of islands are related to those of the nearest continent or other nearby islands, even when the islands' physical conditions resemble those of a different, more distant region (e.g. Galapagos to America, Cape Verde to Africa).

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: indeed it is an almost universal rule that the endemic productions of islands are related to those of the nearest continent, or of other near islands.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter XII, “Geographical Distribution, continued”; section “On the relation of the inhabitants of islands to those of the nearest mainland”. Scope: endemic plants and animals of oceanic islands

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch12-12: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.81

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Biogeographic affinity, proximity and environmental similarity are measurable with open global data. Coverage is broad but not complete for poorly known taxa, and extinction can hide the true source.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For native island endemics, compare phylogenetic distance to biotas of the nearest continent and other islands with distance to environmentally most similar remote regions. The claim is supported if nearest-source affinity predominates across clades and archipelagos.

fields.value:

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Nearest-continent versus climate-matched distant region is a direct decision rule, and public occurrences, climate layers and a synthetic tree supply the variables for well-studied archipelagos. Coverage falls well short of every endemic plant and animal, so the 'almost universal' scope is only partly in reach. Where trees and inventories exist, multiple colonizations and missing mainland sisters are manageable biases rather than fatal ones.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For oceanic-island endemics, compare phylogenetic distance to relatives on the nearest continent or nearby islands with distance to biotas in climatically more similar but geographically farther regions. The claim is confirmed if nearest-source relatives are closer in a large majority of well-sampled clades, and refuted if climate-matching distant regions win about as often.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Ocean currents and wind can make the biologically accessible source differ from the nearest shoreline.

Extinct source populations on the nearest continent can make a living relative look farther away than the historical source.

Most invertebrate and many plant endemics are still missing from phylogenetic trees, so the testable set is biased toward vertebrates and well-studied floras.

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: For endemic vascular plants of oceanic islands, the nearest relatives outside the island group on an independent synthetic phylogeny are, in a large majority of cases, native to the nearest continent or to the island group's own neighbouring islands.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: Island endemics were WCVP accepted species whose native records all fall in one of the 12 pre-registered island groups (3,928 species in 871 genera). All accepted species of those genera were matched exactly to Open Tree and the induced subtree of the synthetic tree was fetched per genus (783 trees). For each endemic in a genus tree that has species outside the island group (2,918 endemics), the outside relatives were the non-island tips of the smallest clade containing the endemic and at least one outside species; the endemic was near-related if more than half of them are native to the nearest continent (TDWG level 1) or the island group's own level-2 region. Shares per island group and pooled were compared with the pre-registered thresholds; the share of all outside congeners native to the near source is reported as a control, and the subset whose nearest outside clade is a single species is reported as a post-hoc check.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered: endemics of island group A = WCVP accepted non-hybrid species whose non-doubtful native records (introduced = 0) all lie in A. For each genus containing such an endemic, all WCVP accepted species are matched exactly to Open Tree (TNRS, context 'Land plants') and the induced subtree of the synthetic tree is fetched. For a focal endemic, the outside relatives O are the non-A tips of the smallest clade containing the focal tip and >= 1 non-A tip. The focal endemic is 'near-related' if more than half of O have a native record in A's pre-registered near source S_A (the TDWG level-1 continent nearest to A, plus A's own TDWG level-2 region, i.e. other near islands). s_A = fraction near-related. Island groups with < 10 focal endemics are dropped. SUPPORTS ('almost universal rule') if pooled s >= 0.75 AND s_A >= 0.6 in at least 75% of remaining island groups.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered: REFUTES if pooled s < 0.5 or if s_A < 0.5 in a majority of remaining island groups. Any other outcome is MIXED. Fewer than 5 island groups remaining: inconclusive (underpowered). WCVP or Open Tree unreachable: inconclusive (data-unavailable). As a descriptive control, the fraction of all non-A congeners native to S_A is reported for each island group.

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: pooled fraction of island endemics whose nearest outside relatives (smallest clade on the Open Tree genus subtree) are mostly native to the nearest continent or the island group's own region

fields.label: Uncertainty
fields.value: island groups with s >= 0.6: 0/12; with s < 0.5: 9/12; endemics scored: 2918

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: 'Related to those of the nearest continent, or of other near islands' is read as: the closest non-island relatives (sister clade on the genus tree) are native to the nearest continent, with near islands meaning the TDWG level-2 region the island group belongs to. Nearest continents (TDWG level 1) are fixed in advance by great-circle proximity: Galápagos 8 (Southern America), Juan Fernández 8, Cape Verde 2 (Africa), Canaries 2, Madeira 2, Azores 1 (Europe), Hawaii 7 (Northern America), Bermuda 7, Mascarenes (MAU+REU+ROD) 2, Seychelles 2, Tristan da Cunha 2, Fiji 5 (Australasia). Darwin's own contrast with climatically similar distant regions (assessors' suggestion) is not modelled; the test asks only whether the nearest continent dominates. Plants only; genus-level trees, so endemics of island-endemic genera are not scored.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value:
World Checklist of Vascular Plants (WCVP), Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew: wcvp_names.csv and wcvp_distribution.csv

Open Tree of Life synthetic tree opentree16.1 via the v3 API: tnrs/match_names (context Land plants, exact) and tree_of_life/induced_subtree

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
The pre-registered criterion is met for refutation (pooled near-related share 0.29; 9 of 12 island groups below 0.5, none at or above 0.6), but this mostly reflects the resolution of the synthetic tree rather than biogeography: the median nearest outside clade contains 80 species, because species absent from every input phylogeny are placed as unresolved members of their genus, so the majority rule then scores the geographic spread of the whole genus. In most groups the near-related share barely exceeds the share of all outside congeners native to the near source (e.g. Galápagos 0.54 vs 0.53; Juan Fernández 0.33 vs 0.31), i.e. the test has little power beyond genus membership.

Post hoc (not pre-registered): among the 313 endemics whose nearest outside relative is a single resolved species, 63% are near-related, and Darwin's rule holds well for the Canaries (0.83, n = 77), Galápagos (0.90, n = 10), Mascarenes (0.91, n = 57), Madeira (0.73, n = 22) and Juan Fernández (0.67, n = 12), but fails for Hawaii (0.23, n = 74) and Fiji (0.43, n = 35), whose floras derive largely from Malesia, Australasia and the Pacific rather than from the nearest continent. This post-hoc pattern does not change the verdict but suggests the claim holds for Atlantic and Indian Ocean islands near continents and fails for remote Pacific archipelagos.

'Near islands' was operationalised as the island group's own TDWG level-2 region; for Hawaii and Fiji this excludes other Pacific archipelagos that Darwin might count as near islands, which makes these groups harder to pass.

Darwin's specific contrast (Galápagos with America rather than with climatically similar Cape Verde, and vice versa) was not modelled; the test only asks whether the nearest continent dominates.

Plants only; genus-level trees, so endemics of island-endemic genera (e.g. many Hawaiian lobeliads) were not scored.
